transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-15
Start time: 16:00 PST
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Nina Jacobs (Redwood SE), Laura Kim (Pinecap - Head of Platform), Tom Reyes (Pinecap - CTO), Maya Singh (Pinecap - DevOps), Evan Cho (Pinecap - PM)

Summary:
Quick product walkthrough focused on rate limiting, quota controls, and multi-tenant keys (org vs project). Customer is evaluating options for protecting shared inference endpoints across internal teams and external partners; key concerns: per-project billing/visibility, burst allowances, priority tiers, and security (KMS, audit logs, SSO). Redwood demo included Console UI and brief API examples.

Topics:
- Org-level vs project-level API keys and scoping
- Rate limiting strategies (per-key vs per-route, token quotas, burst/steady-state)
- Quotas, reservations, and tiering for multi-tenant setups
- Security: audit logs, KMS, SOC2, SSO/SAML and RBAC
- Next steps: pricing, security docs, pilot benchmark

Transcript:
[00:00] Samir: Okay, thanks everyone for joining, I'll do a super quick intro, I'm Samir, AE on the account, and with me is Nina our solutions engineer, we'll walk through rate limits and org/project keys and how customers typically set them up. Laura, Tom, Maya, Evan, thanks for making time.
[00:18] Laura: Hey Samir, yeah thanks. We're trying to figure out how to let our internal teams and a few external partners hit a single Redwood endpoint without one team bringing down cost or latency for others. So segregation of usage and billing visibility are a big item.
[00:32] Nina: Totally, that's exactly what the org/project keys model is for — you get an org root with billing and org-level SLOs and then per-project keys for teams, each with quotas and rate limits. We'll open the console in a sec.
[00:45] Tom: Quick Q up front — can we set both token quotas and request-per-minute limits? Sometimes we do long completions and want token-based throttles not just RPM.
[00:56] Nina: Yes, you can set quotas by tokens and by requests. We support per-key token quotas, per-route limits, and global org limits. There's also a burst allowance parameter so short spikes are handled without hard 429s immediately.
[01:14] Evan: And how does that behave for reserved capacity vs hosted? Our plan may be to mix dedicated and hosted nodes.
[01:22] Samir: Great question — for Dedicated (reserved capacity) you can reserve baseline throughput and set soft/ hard caps on projects; Redwood will route to dedicated first then fallback to hosted with a policy you can control. We can demo the policy UI.
[01:36] Maya: Are the fallbacks automatic? We need predictable SLAs for production traffic.
[01:41] Nina: Fallbacks are policy-driven. You can configure auto-fallback to a cheaper model variant or to hosted pool, and choose whether to surface a 429 to the client or queue with degraded latency.
[01:52] Tom: Sounds good. Can you show the console now?
[01:55] Nina: Sure, I'll screenshare. (screen share sound) Ok opening the console — top nav, team -> org settings -> rate limiting.
[02:08] Nina: Here you can see the org overview: total tokens this mo, active projects, and alerts for near-quota projects. You can click into Project: 'Dev-Platform' and see a per-key breakdown.
[02:19] Laura: That breakdown is nice — shows per-route token consumption. Can we export that to our billing system?
[02:25] Samir: Yep we have a usage export API and webhooks for near-quota alerts; customers often push those into internal billing pipelines. We'll include the usage export doc.
[02:36] [02:36] Nina: Now under project keys, you create keys scoped to routes and TTLs - you can limit a key to embeddings-only, or generation routes only, and set 'tokens per month' and 'reqs per minute'.
[02:50] Evan: Is the keys model hierarchical? Like can a project inherit org policies but override them?
[02:55] Nina: Yes — org sets defaults (global limit, soft thresholds), project keys inherit but can have stricter limits. The UI indicates inherited vs overridden values.
[03:07] Tom: How are throttles enforced under the hood? Is it token-bucket?
[03:12] Nina: It's a hybrid. We use a leaky/token bucket for per-key burst control plus steady-state rate enforcement at the route level. For dedicated pools we also factor in reserved capacity so you don't oversubscribe.
[03:27] Laura: Any concerns about clock skew across regions? We have teams in EU & US.
[03:32] Nina: We do region-aware enforcement and keep counters at the org edge in each region; there's eventual consistency but thresholds are conservative to avoid accidental over-usage. We can share the architectural note.
[03:43] Maya: On security, we need SSO and audit logs, plus keys should be stored in our KMS if possible.
[03:48] Samir: For Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS/HSM. For hosted, we offer envelope encryption with customer-managed keys (bring your own key), and full audit logs that record key usage, IPs, and user. We'll share the SOC2 pack and the KMS integration guide.
[04:03] Tom: Does the audit log show per-request metadata? We need to tie calls back to internal request IDs for troubleshooting.
[04:09] Nina: Yes, logs can include request-id headers (you can pass X-Request-ID), model, tokens consumed, latency, and which project key was used. Logs are exportable to S3 or to our SIEM integrations.
[04:24] Evan: What about RBAC for who can create project keys? We have platform admins vs product teams.
[04:29] Nina: RBAC is supported; roles at org and project level (admin, billing, viewer, developer). We also support SAML SSO provisioning.
[04:38] Laura: Ok demo looks promising. Can you show how limits surface in the API responses? We want to handle 429s gracefully.
[04:46] Nina: Yup — example API response shows 429 plus a header X-RateLimit-Reset and a Retry-After. We also provide a 'quota_remaining' header for tokens and requests. Error payloads sometimes vary based on client library.
[04:58] Samir: Important note — we recommend exponential backoff and a small jitter. We also have SDK-level retries you can opt into.
[05:08] Tom: Do you support per-route priorities? For example, routing chat completions before embeddings if system-critical?
[05:14] Nina: You can set priority tags on keys and on routes; routing honors priority then cost/latency policies. For dedicated capacity you can also reserve throughput by priority.
[05:24] Maya: Can we have partner tenants limited to a small monthly token allotment but allowed short bursts?
[05:30] Nina: Absolutely — set a monthly token quota plus a burst allowance bucket; after bursts exceed, you'll get throttles. You can optionally configure soft-limits that send alerts but don't cut traffic.
[05:41] Evan: About billing labels — can project-level usage map to our internal billing codes?
[05:46] Samir: Yes, you can add metadata tags to projects and keys; the usage export includes tags so your billing ETL can map to cost centers.
[05:55] Laura: Any caveats with embeddings? They tend to have different token math.
[05:59] Nina: Embeddings are tracked as token units too but we surface embedding-specific metrics (vectors/requests) in the console. You can set separate quotas for embeddings if you want.
[06:12] Tom: What's the typical time to set up org/projects and keys for a new customer?
[06:16] Samir: Self-serve customers can do it in minutes; for Private or Dedicated we'll help with setup — onboarding usually 1-2 weeks for dedicated capacity provisioning.
[06:28] Maya: If we start with hosted and later move to dedicated, how do keys/mappings migrate?
[06:33] Nina: Keys are logical and not tied to underlying infra. You update routing policy to point a project to a Dedicated pool; keys remain the same. There's a small window during cutover which you can configure to avoid double-billing.
[06:47] Evan: Do you have rate limit SDK examples for Node and Python?
[06:51] Nina: Yes we have SDK examples including automatic retries and quota headers. I'll paste links after the call.
[06:57] [06:57] Tom: Can we do per-tenant rate limiting for external partners with separate billing? We want each partner to be meter-billed.
[07:03] Samir: Yes — create a project per partner and give them project-scoped keys. Usage maps to that project for billing exports and invoices.
[07:12] Laura: Great. Let's talk about spikes — last year we had a sudden load and a third-party job kept retrying, blowing through our quotas. How can we prevent runaway retries?
[07:23] Nina: A few patterns: 1) set soft limits and alerts so ops see it before it becomes hard; 2) set per-key per-minute caps; 3) set client side request throttling + server-side 429 + Retry-After; 4) blacklist keys if abused. We also support anomaly detection for unusual token growth.
[07:45] Evan: Anomaly detection sounds useful — is it built-in?
[07:48] Nina: Built-in alerts with heuristics; advanced anomaly detection is an add-on in Redwood Optimize, which can tie regressions to prompt sets and send alerts.
[07:58] Tom: Let's talk compliance — SOC2, data residency. Some of our clients require EU-only processing.
[08:06] Samir: For data residency we have region routing and private deployments; you can enforce region restriction on a project so all requests are routed to EU-only pools. For strict requirements, Private deployment or on-prem is available. We'll include the region routing doc.
[08:20] Maya: Our security team will want to review key rotation process.
[08:24] Nina: Key rotation is supported via key versioning — you can rotate and set a grace period for old keys. Rotations are auditable in the logs.
[08:35] Laura: Ok good. Can you show an API example of creating a project key with token quota?
[08:40] Nina: Sure, here's a curl snippet — POST /orgs/:org/projects/:proj/keys with body {"name":"partner-a","scopes":["generation"],"tokens_per_month":500000,"requests_per_minute":60}. The response includes the key id and the masked secret.
[09:00] Evan: Masked secret — what's key storage like?
[09:03] Nina: Secrets are stored encrypted, and for Private you can point to your KMS. For hosted we support BYOK (bring your own key) so the master key is customer-managed.
[09:14] Tom: Any rate limit differences for streaming APIs? We have streaming chat with long-lived connections.
[09:19] Nina: Streaming is tracked differently; we consider tokens emitted and active connections. You can set concurrent session caps. For streaming you might use concurrency limits + token quotas.
[09:31] Laura: Do you provide per-token cost estimates in the console? Our finance folks need cost visibility per project.
[09:36] Samir: Yes, cost is broken down by project, model, and route. You can export cost reports weekly or monthly.
[09:44] Evan: What about automated throttle notifications to Slack or PagerDuty?
[09:48] Nina: We support webhooks and native integrations to Slack and PagerDuty for alerts. You can configure thresholds that trigger notifications or incident creation.
[09:58] Tom: We need to run a pilot with realistic load. How do we set it up?
[10:02] Samir: We typically do a benchmark run: Redwood spins up a pilot pool, we run your load generator against dev keys and collect latency, p50/p95/p99, and token burn. Nina can coordinate.
[10:12] Nina: I'll propose a bench plan in the follow-up. For the pilot we usually want representative prompt sets and traffic patterns — short chat traffic and long completions if you have both.
[10:24] Maya: Timezones — we might need multiple benchmark windows.
[10:27] Nina: Totally fine. We'll coordinate.
[10:31] [10:31] Laura: Any pitfalls you typically see?
[10:34] Samir: A few: 1) Not tagging projects properly so billing gets messy; 2) letting long-running background jobs use prod keys — use separate project keys for batch jobs; 3) relying solely on request rate limits without token quotas for long completions.
[10:50] Evan: Good call. Could we briefly discuss enforcement semantics — when a token quota is exceeded mid-stream does the call get cut or allowed and billed overage?
[11:01] Nina: You can configure behavior: hard cut (immediate 429), soft cut (finish request but log overage and bill), or throttled (degraded model fallback). We'll show the settings UI.
[11:15] Nina: (navigates) Under Project Settings -> Quota Behavior you can pick enforcement mode and set overage pricing if desired.
[11:25] Tom: We need predictable cost, so soft overage might be risky. Can we auto-redirect to a cheaper model instead?
[11:31] Nina: Yes, model fallback is common — e.g., if gpt-x is out of budget, fall back to gpt-lite. You can also set hard caps with alerted soft thresholds.
[11:44] Maya: For tenant isolation, is there per-project caching? We use prefix caching heavily.
[11:50] Nina: We offer prefix/KV cache per project so one team's cache doesn't contaminate another. Cache hits are accounted to the project that originated the request.
[12:02] Evan: Are cache settings adjustable per project? TTLs etc?
[12:05] Nina: Per-project TTLs and namespace isolation, yes.
[12:09] Laura: Can you walk through creating a partner project and issuing keys?
[12:13] Nina: Sure — create Project 'partner-acme' -> Tags: external, partner -> Create key: scope generation, tokens per month 200k, RPM 30 -> rotate after 90 days -> Save. Key created. (typing) The key appears masked, you copy it once.
[12:35] Tom: Good. How do we restrict a key to only embeddings endpoints?
[12:39] Nina: During key creation you choose scopes: embeddings, generation, rerank, etc. The token validation checks the route and rejects disallowed calls.
[12:49] Evan: For testing, can we issue temporary TTL keys?
[12:52] Nina: Yes TTL keys supported; great for ephemeral partner access or CI runners.
[12:58] Laura: Security question: if a key is leaked, can we trace usage and block quickly?
[13:04] Nina: Yes, audit logs show per-request metadata; you can revoke the key immediately and optionally blacklist the IPs. We also support key compromised workflows where we rotate and issue replacements.
[13:18] Samir: We should run through a concrete pilot plan: Redwood to run a benchmark, share pricing for reserved vs hosted, and hand over security docs. Thoughts?
[13:26] Laura: Sounds right. We also need a test matrix: partner traffic, background jobs, streaming, and embeddings.
[13:32] Nina: I'll assemble a test matrix template and share with you.
[13:37] Tom: Any limits on number of projects? We might have dozens.
[13:41] Samir: No hard limits — orgs can create many projects. Very large numbers we can support with best practices.
[13:47] Evan: About SLA — do rate limit errors count against uptime?
[13:52] Samir: Rate limits are enforcement behavior and not an availability outage. SLA applies to infra availability; we also offer policies to avoid being rate-limited by reserving capacity.
[14:03] Maya: Ok can you email the sample pricing?
[14:06] Samir: Will do. We'll include cost example for a partner project with 200k tokens/month and 30 RPM.
[14:14] Laura: We have one more question on audit retention. Our compliance team needs 365 days of logs.
[14:19] Nina: Default retention is 90 days but enterprise plans support 1 year or longer. We can include retention options in the security doc.
[14:29] Tom: What about SSO SCIM provisioning?
[14:33] Nina: SCIM for user provisioning is supported for enterprise customers.
[14:37] Evan: Any special considerations for dedicated/private deployments?
[14:41] Samir: On Private we give full network and KMS control; rate limits and keys are same model but enforced by your private control plane. On-prem requires lightweight install and we help with ops.
[14:53] Laura: Can we see a sample alert for near-quota?
[14:56] Nina: (navigates) Here's an alert rule: threshold 80% tokens, condition sustained 5m, triggers webhook -> Slack channel #ops -> severity P2.
[15:08] Maya: How are retries represented in the metrics? We want to avoid counting retries as unique requests in billing if they are client retries.
[15:14] Nina: Retries are requests; we recommend idempotency keys for retries and client-side backoff. We can show patterns to minimize wasted tokens.
[15:26] Tom: For long-running jobs, can we schedule off-peak quotas at night?
[15:30] Nina: You can define time-based rules — e.g., higher quotas during off-peak windows or allow burst credits to accumulate.
[15:40] Evan: Can we set different quotas per environment (dev/stage/prod) under same org?
[15:44] Nina: Yes, create projects for each environment and apply different quotas/tags.
[15:51] Laura: Anything else?
[15:53] Samir: Quick recap — action items we'll follow up with pricing, security docs, and pilot plan. Nina will schedule the benchmark.
[16:00] Tom: Perfect. We'll confirm pilot stakeholders.
[16:03] Evan: One last small ask — sample webhook payload for near-quota so our infra can parse it.
[16:08] Nina: I'll include that in the follow-up.
[16:12] Laura: Thanks everyone, this was helpful.
[16:15] Samir: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the doc pack.

End of transcript.
